These shares describe this screening design and the levels chosen for it, not the general importance of each kind of choice. Averaged over the other factors and both models, asking the model to decide on van Allen • The multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis every code raised MCC by 0.063 (95% interval 0.036 to 0.093) and high reasoning effort raised it by 0.051 (0.028 to 0.073), whereas dividing the codebook into five parts lowered it by 0.045 (-0.066 to -0.024). Luna exceeded Haiku by 0.038 (0.015 to 0.061). In contrast, the paraphrased instructions (-0.012; -0.028 to 0.003) and the shuffled code order (0.012; 0.000 to 0.023) changed agreement little (Supplementary Table S4 and Figure S1).

4.5 Interactions and changes in coding behaviour

The design factors interacted (Figure 5). The 'decide every code' instructions raised MCC by 0.10 when the whole codebook was sent in one request but by only 0.02 when it was divided. Interestingly, under 'find passages', dividing the codebook changed agreement little on average (-0.004), whereas under 'decide every code' it lowered MCC by 0.086. High effort mattered mainly under 'find passages' (0.087, against 0.016 under 'decide every code'), and there mainly for Haiku (0.14, against 0.03 for Luna). An apparent interaction between wording and code order (0.032; 0.016 to 0.050) is aliased with the three-way interaction of instructions, division, and effort. The factors were associated with changes in how many BCTs the models coded. Asking the model to decide on every code added about five BCTs per report, raising sensitivity by 0.27 and lowering precision by 0.11, while dividing the codebook added about three BCTs per report and lowered precision by 0.13. Because the reference records 5.7 BCTs per report, most additional codings counted as false positives, whether they were errors or fell outside the reference's scope; the data cannot distinguish a change in the propensity to apply codes from improved coverage or different interpretations of the codes.

4.6 Cost

The recorded cost of a run ranged from US$0.12 to US$0.87 per 40 reports, and every configuration on the cost-agreement frontier was a Luna run (Figure 6). Luna with 'decide every code', the whole codebook, and low effort (cell 09) reached MCC 0.564 for US$0.18, against 0.573 for US$0.28 for the highest-scoring configuration. For context, the original Sol and Sonnet runs reached 0.576 on the same reports at about 18 and 28 times the cost of cell 09. On average, dividing the codebook added US$0.32 per 40 reports and lowered agreement, whereas high effort added US$0.15 and raised agreement, mainly under the 'find passages' instructions.

4.7 Scoring choices and individual codes

Ranking the 32 configurations by F1 rather than MCC changed the order little (Spearman's ρ = 0.97), but ranking them by balanced accuracy changed it substantially (ρ = 0.54) and selected a different best configuration. The effects of instructions and effort kept their direction under both secondary scoring scopes (Figure 7). However, the effect of dividing the codebook did not keep its size; it was larger at the level of taxonomy groups (-0.072) and largely disappeared on the 12 prioritized BCTs (-0.011; -0.037 to 0.016). van Allen • The multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis five-part codebook shrank from -0.045 over all 94 BCTs to -0.011 over the 12 prioritized BCTs.

The models coded whole reports, including Discussion sections, against all 94 codes, whereas the historical annotators excluded Discussion sections and techniques not directed at the target behaviour. Units without an annotation were scored as absent, although the reference does not record which were assessed and judged absent, so the scopes partly change the evaluation target. Supplementary Table S4 gives all contrasts under each scope.

Agreement for individual BCTs also depended heavily on configuration (Supplementary Table S5). For example, among the 11 BCTs annotated in at least five screening reports, sensitivity for 3.1 Social support (unspecified) ranged from 0.06 to 0.88 across configurations, whereas 5.3 Information about social and environmental consequences was never found in more than 29% of the reports annotated with it.

4.8 Combining runs

A strict majority vote over repeat runs raised agreement modestly, and a vote across models raised it more (Supplementary Table S6). Compared with the mean of their constituent runs, the vote of the four original models gained 0.052 and the vote of the eight Haiku and Luna cell 09 runs gained 0.055. However, compared with the strongest configuration they combined, the gains were smaller, at 0.048 (0.014 to 0.083) and 0.017 (-0.015 to 0.048), respectively. Voting worked by trading sensitivity for precision. For example, for the four Haiku repeats, counting a BCT as present when any run coded it gave 11.3 BCTs per report and MCC 0.474, whereas the majority rule gave 5.7 BCTs per report and MCC 0.521.

4.9 Reports excluded from screening

The four original runs, which had similar agreement on the screening reports (0.563 to 0.577), diverged on the 50 reports excluded from screening (Figure 8). Sonnet's agreement rose to 0.636, while Haiku, Luna, and Sol scored from 0.541 to 0.575; Sonnet also had the highest agreement on all 95 reports, as reported before the screen (Supplementary Table S7). The majority vote of the four models reached 0.647 on the excluded reports, exceeding Haiku by 0.106 (0.084 to 0.129), Sol by 0.081 (0.052 to 0.112), and Luna by 0.072 (0.036 to 0.107). Its agreement was similar to Sonnet's (difference 0.010; -0.014 to 0.035), although the study was not designed to test equivalence. The vote coded 6.7 BCTs per report, against 7.3 to 9.5 for the single models and 5.6 in the reference. S7.

5 Discussion

5.1 Principal findings

This study sought to describe the analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis and to explore a first part of it, using a screening design on a public dataset. Three findings stand out.

First, choices interacted. Within this design, the contrasts for task instructions, reasoning effort, and codebook division were each larger than the average difference between the two tested models, and the effect of each depended on the others and on the model; for example, asking the model to decide on every code helped most when the whole codebook was sent at once. Said another way, a comparison of models at one fixed configuration answers a narrower question than it appears to. The tested paraphrase and code shuffle changed agreement little, although one paraphrase and one shuffle are thin samples of those spaces, and meaning-preserving changes have had much larger effects elsewhere (Sclar et al., 2024).

Second, part of the variation in agreement was variation in alignment with a particular reference. The design factors acted mainly by changing how many codes the models applied, while the reference annotated 5.7 BCTs per report under rules that excluded Discussion sections and techniques not directed at the target behaviour. Configurations that coded more were therefore penalized partly for codings outside the reference's coverage, not only for errors, and the apparent cost of dividing the codebook shrank from -0.045 over all 94 BCTs to -0.011 on the 12 BCTs the annotators prioritized. Majority voting worked through the same channel, bringing the number of codes per report closer to the reference's. Agreement statistics alone cannot distinguish error from misalignment.

Third, rankings were not stable. Ranking configurations by balanced accuracy rather than MCC selected a different best configuration, although this partly reflects a different objective, because balanced accuracy rewards the sensitivity gained by coding more. Unfortunately, the 40 screening reports also proved a poor guide to model rankings; four models with similar agreement on them diverged on the 50 excluded reports. In hindsight, the bootstrap intervals on the screening reports were already wide enough to warn that similar point estimates on 40 reports were weak evidence of equivalence. Nonetheless, a vote across the four models had agreement similar to the best of them on the excluded reports without requiring the analyst to know in advance which model was best, a practical hedge when model rankings are uncertain, although it costs as much as all four runs together. Voting across samples is an established way to make language model outputs more reliable (Wang et al., 2023); here, voting across different models helped more than voting across repeats of one model.

5.2 Implications for practice and reporting

For teams using AI-assisted coding, the results suggest four practices. First, prompts, model identifiers, settings, task scope, and scoring rules should be reported in full, and the choices with the largest contrasts here (instructions, codebook presentation, and reasoning effort) warrant sensitivity analyses. Provider defaults are themselves choices; for example, the original Haiku run with the provider's default effort reached 0.563, whereas the cell 09 runs with low effort set explicitly averaged 0.489, although a change of software version also separates them. Second, at least one configuration should be repeated, and unitlevel agreement between repeats reported alongside summary agreement; where individual codings are reviewed and used as evidence, the instability of individual decisions matters more than the stability of the summary. Third, where the reference's scope differs from the coding task, results should also be reported for a scoring scope that matches the reference's coverage. Finally, the primary agreement statistic should be chosen in advance together with the objective it represents, and a configuration or model should be chosen on some documents and confirmed on others. For methodologists and editors, these forks are candidates for required sensitivity analyses in reporting guidance on AI-assisted qualitative analysis, and a small specification curve is now inexpensive to produce; this screen cost US$13.66 in recorded API spend.

5.3 Related work and a second dataset

These results extend evidence that configuration choices can change the conclusions of LLM-based annotation (Sclar et al., 2024; Baumann et al., 2025; Messing, 2026) to deductive qualitative coding with a large codebook. In this setting, the choices with the largest contrasts were structural (i.e., whether every code must be decided, and how the codebook is presented) rather than matters of wording. A companion study applied the same tools to 17 interviews coded against 115 codes from the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and its Outcomes Addendum (Damschroder et al., 2022a (Damschroder et al., , 2022b)), with an earlier model-assisted coding as the reference, and observed a similar pattern, in that 'decide every code' improved agreement more when the whole codebook was sent at once (manuscript in preparation; the parent study is described by Radhakrishnan et al., 2026). Those results are not part of the evidence presented here.

5.4 Limitations

This research is subject to several limitations worth noting when interpreting the findings. First, agreement is not validity, and here the reference and the coding task differed in scope (Section 3.2). Treating units that were not annotated as absences counts as errors some codings that a reviewer might accept, and references have their own blind spots (Liu et al., 2026). A blinded review of a stratified sample of disagreements would show how much of the measured disagreement reflects error rather than differences in scope; I did not undertake one here, and it is a priority for future work. Second, the screen used one dataset of published English-language trial reports, which the models may have seen during training, and two low-cost models; effects for stronger models are unknown because the focus stage was not run. Third, it used 40 reports, and model rankings on them did not hold on the reports excluded from screening. Fourth, repeat-run variation was measured for one configuration per model, and the bootstrap intervals do not include it. Fifth, the half fraction aliases each two-way interaction with a three-way interaction, and each incidental factor was represented by a single alternative. Finally, the analyses of combining runs and of excluded reports were added after the screen and are exploratory, and specific models and prices will date quickly (Chen et al., 2024). Taken together, these limitations argue for treating the specific estimates reported here as hypothesis generating rather than definitive; the aim is to learn which kinds of choice matter, which should outlast any one model.

5.5 A research agenda

One dataset cannot establish which choices matter in general; that requires evidence from many datasets, frameworks, and kinds of text. I therefore propose a research agenda that others can take up independently, with the aim of advancing the methodology of AI-assisted qualitative analysis rather than validating any one tool or model. The questions I consider most pressing are 1) which forks account for most of the variation in agreement, and whether their ordering holds across datasets and frameworks; 2) whether model rankings survive changes to instructions, codebook presentation, scoring, and the documents scored; 3) which properties of a code (e.g., its prevalence, abstraction, and overlap with other codes) predict whether its agreement is robust; and 4) whether conclusions drawn from agreement hold when the quality of coding is judged directly (Liu et al., 2026).

Progress on these questions does not require a coordinated project, only studies that can be compared. To this end, I suggest that researchers who evaluate AI-assisted coding against existing human coding declare their multiverse before running it, include at least the choices with the largest contrasts here (task instructions, codebook presentation, and reasoning effort), repeat at least one configuration, and report the six quantities in Section 2.5 together with the declaration. QualFrame, QualBench, and the declaration and scripts used here are openly available and can be adapted to other data. Studies reported in this way could later be combined across datasets and frameworks (Supplementary Section S5).

6 Conclusions

In a first screen of the analytic multiverse of AI-assisted directed content analysis, choices about task instructions, codebook presentation, and reasoning effort produced larger contrasts in agreement with historical human annotation than the difference between two models, interacted with one another and with the model, and changed which configuration looked best. The apparent effect of one choice also depended on which annotations were treated as the reference. Repeat runs, reports excluded from screening, more than one agreement statistic, and more than one scoring scope were each needed to see this. General lessons will require many datasets coded by people, and comparable multiverse studies, run independently and reported in a common format, are an important first step towards them. Before AIassisted coding can be relied on as a research instrument, we must establish how much its results depend on the choices made in configuring it.

S2 Analysis details and deviations from the plan

Variance decomposition. The variance decomposition partitioned the sum of squares of the 32 configuration MCCs into a saturated set of orthogonal contrasts (i.e., one contrast for each degree of freedom): model, the five main effects, the ten two-way interactions, and the interaction of model with each of these. Its shares depend on the models, levels, prompts, corpus, and scoring rules chosen and are not general variance components. I compared the decomposition with the variance expected from run-torun noise, using the pooled standard deviation of the repeat runs and assuming that run-to-run variation elsewhere in the design resembled that of cell 09. Among the differences between models, the largest was in the effect of reasoning effort (5.2% of the variation), and the main effects of instruction wording and code order together accounted for 1.5%.

Code-level robustness. For BCTs annotated in at least five of the 40 reports, code-level robustness was described by the range of sensitivity across configurations and the median rate at which configurations coded the BCT in reports where it was not annotated (Table S5).

Unlocated quotations.

Because the scoring tables record quotation location by run rather than by unit, I bounded the influence of unlocated quotations on each main effect; that is, I assumed that every unlocated passage was the only support for a distinct applied unit, and removed those units as true or false positives in whichever direction most changed the effect (Table S3).

Deviations from the plan. The declared plan differed from what was done in six respects. First, the noise-floor repeats were declared at each model's preset effort, which for Haiku matched no design cell; before running, they were changed to explicit low effort so that the repeats replicate cell 09. Second, connection errors interrupted 13 requests, and the affected runs were resumed as described in Section S1.

Third, the focus stage with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol was costed but not run. Fourth, the analyses of combining runs and of excluded reports were added after screening. Fifth, the compliance summaries and the bound for unlocated quotations were also added after screening. Finally, with a single dataset I used the factorial decomposition described above rather than the multilevel model described in Section S5.

S3 Output compliance and robustness checks

Of 12,986 quoted passages, 193 (1.5%) could not be located in the report; these ranged from none to 4.7% per run and were slightly more common under 'decide every code' (1.6%) than under 'find passages' (1.2%). Required decisions were missing for 77 units (0.09% of units under 'decide every code'), 63 of which came from one run. Table S2 summarizes output compliance by model and instructions. Truncation was not recorded separately; however, under 'decide every code', a truncated response would appear as missing decisions. Table S3 bounds the influence of unlocated quotations on each main effect, and the largest change in any run's MCC under the worst-case assumption was 0.048.

S5 Contributing comparable multiverse studies

Suitable data. Interviews, focus groups, open-text survey responses, or documents coded against a codebook or framework (e.g., the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, the Theoretical Domains Framework, a behaviour change taxonomy, or a team's own codebook) are suitable, together with the codebook as the coders used it and, ideally, each coder's independent decisions before reconciliation as well as the agreed coding. Ethics approval and participant consent must allow the text to be processed by an AI service.

Running a study.

A team can install QualFrame, adapt the declaration used here or write its own, and run it on its own computers, sending text only to the AI services its approvals allow. QualBench scores the runs locally against the team's coding, so the configuration contrasts and their uncertainty can be reported without sharing raw text. Beyond its contribution to the agenda, such a study gives a team a benchmark of how AI coding compares with its own coding, code by code, and of which configurations worked best for its data and at what cost.

Combining studies.

Studies that report comparable contrasts with their uncertainty could later be combined in a hierarchical meta-analysis, with datasets as the unit of replication and frameworks kept distinct, because codes from different frameworks are not common categories. Where unit-level decisions are available, agreement at the level of document × code decisions can also be modelled with fixed effects for design factors, random effects for incidental choices, and random effects for documents and codes nested within datasets, following Messing (2026); such a model yields variance shares for each factor and interaction, and indicates whether additional prompt variants, repeats, or documents would most reduce uncertainty.

What it could show.

Imagine that several research teams, each holding interviews or documents already coded against a different framework, independently run comparable multiverses on their own data and report the same contrasts. If the advantage of deciding on every code held across datasets and frameworks, this would suggest a general property of how current models apply codebooks, and could inform default settings in tools and reporting guidance. If instead the best configuration varied by framework or by kind of text, this would suggest that configurations should be tuned and confirmed for each project, and that reporting guidance should require such confirmation.

S1 Software, instructions, and execution

QualBench measures. At the level of document × code units, QualBench reports MCC and balanced accuracy as primary measures, with sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, Cohen's kappa, Gwet's AC1, and prevalence-and bias-adjusted kappa, and the same measures for two rules that read nothing (every code present and every code absent). It repeats these at the level of parent codes, checks whether each quotation can be found in its document, measures agreement between repeat runs, and reports cost and time.

Screening runner. The screening runner expands a declared multiverse into one locked QualFrame configuration per run, validates every configuration without calling an API, records the software version and commit of each run, and enforces study-level and per-run spending limits. It reserved the worst-case cost of each request against the study limit (US$25) and the per-run limit before sending it, and recorded the cost reported by the provider afterwards. Each run records its software version and commit, and the final screening commit was 595c937, on a development branch of QualFrame 0.11.0.

Instructions and codebook division. Both instruction packages require each quotation to be copied exactly from the report and to occur only once in it. For each package, one paraphrase was drafted with AI assistance and approved by me before any run; it kept the rules, the output format, and the list of codes, but changed the wording and the order of sentences. The five-part division assigned whole taxonomy groups to parts (four of 19 BCTs and one of 18), and each part was sent with the full report in a separate request. Runs with the whole codebook made 40 requests and runs with five parts made 200.

Execution.

The recorded spend of US$13.66 compares with a pre-study estimate of about US$11. Two calibration runs, cell 15 for each model (decide every code, five parts, high effort), were executed first to check the cost model; they cost more than estimated (US$0.81 against US$0.60 for Haiku and US$0.65 against US$0.33 for Luna) but remained within the limits. The remaining runs followed in a random order, so that the time of a run was not confounded with any factor. The per-run spending limit was raised from US$2 to US$3, with my approval, for three Haiku runs with the codebook in five parts. Runs interrupted by connection errors were resumed from their saved state under a bounded resume policy (13 resumes in total) without repeating completed requests. The worst-case reservations for the 13 interrupted requests (US$6.71 in total) remain on the ledger because the provider charges for those attempts are unknown; the recorded spend of US$13.66 excludes them.

Compliance and cost.

Output compliance was summarized as the share of quoted passages that could not be located in the report, the number of code labels outside the codebook, and the number of required decisions missing under 'decide every code' (under 'find passages', codes that were not selected are expected to be absent from the output). Cost per run was the API spend recorded in the budget ledger.

Declarations

Prospective design declaration. The screening design, report sample, prompts, and analysis plan were declared in a configuration file and frozen before any screening call. The declaration was not publicly registered; it is available in the OSF project (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/9287H).
